title: Indian Immigrant Arrested in US With $3 Million in Stolen Tungsten Powder
excerpt: Deepak Kumar, a 31-year-old Fresno trucker, was caught hauling 10 pallets of stolen tungsten oxide from a Mitsubishi shipment and is now in ICE custody in California.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Deepak Kumar, a 31-year-old undocumented immigrant, was arrested with $2.86 million in stolen tungsten oxide.
  • Kumar's valid California commercial driver's license raises concerns about CDL policies for migrants.
  • Tungsten oxide is crucial for military and high-tech applications, highlighting supply chain security issues.
  • Kumar remains in ICE custody as the Trump administration intensifies immigration enforcement in California.
  • The case underscores legal risks for undocumented immigrants, even with state-issued documents.

A 31-year-old undocumented Indian immigrant is in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody after Pennsylvania authorities say he was caught hauling 10 pallets of stolen tungsten oxide powder valued at nearly $2.86 million in his truck.

Deepak Kumar, a Fresno-based trucker, was tracked down and arrested after Mitsubishi Materials Corporation reported that a driver had gone missing with a scheduled shipment of the strategic industrial powder, according to the New York Post.

How the Theft Unfolded

The shipment of tungsten oxide powder — used in armor-piercing ammunition, ceramics, lasers, optical products, and high-tech windows — was scheduled for pickup on June 24 from a Mitsubishi Materials facility. The pickup was delayed by one day, but company officials raised the alarm on June 26 after they could no longer reach the driver.

https://x.com/PoliceIncident/status/2080227620332146721

Investigators deployed a Flock camera, a specialized Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) system, to locate Kumar's truck the following day. When officers stopped him, Kumar presented three forms of identification: an invalid work visa, a fraudulent New York State driver's license, and a valid California commercial driver's license.

He was arrested on theft charges and later transferred to McFarland, California, where he remains in ICE custody. It is not yet clear whether Kumar intended to sell the tungsten oxide or whether the incident involved a communication breakdown with the shipping company, NDTV reported.

California's CDL Policy Under Fire

Kumar's arrest has reignited a politically charged debate over California's policy of issuing commercial driver's licenses to migrants who possess federally issued Employment Authorization Documents (EADs). Kumar was able to legally obtain a California CDL during Governor Gavin Newsom's administration because he held a valid federal work permit at the time.

"Sacramento chose to turn temporary federal work documents into commercial driver's licenses for undocumented immigrants, creating what they call a dangerous loophole."

— Trump administration critics, per New York Post

The Trump administration has repeatedly accused Newsom of making California a "sanctuary state" for truckers. Federal officials argue that the policy allows undocumented immigrants to operate heavy commercial vehicles across state lines with minimal oversight, a concern amplified by cases like Kumar's.

Strategic Material Raises Security Questions

Tungsten oxide is not an ordinary cargo. The powder is classified as a strategic material with military and advanced-technology applications. It is a key component in armor-piercing rounds, high-performance ceramics, laser systems, and specialized optical products. The theft of nearly $3 million worth from a major Japanese multinational has raised questions about supply chain security for sensitive industrial materials in the United States.

The incident comes at a time when federal authorities are increasingly focused on the security of critical material supply chains, particularly those with defense applications.

Part of a Broader Immigration Crackdown

Kumar's case is one of several recent arrests that federal immigration authorities have highlighted as part of the Trump administration's intensified enforcement campaign, particularly in California. The US Border Patrol's El Centro Sector this week separately announced the arrest of an undocumented Mexican agricultural worker in Thermal, California, who had prior charges including rape and assault with a deadly weapon.

For the Indian diaspora, the case underscores the legal risks facing undocumented immigrants in the US, where even those holding valid state-issued documents can face federal immigration enforcement. Immigration attorneys have long warned that state-level protections do not shield individuals from federal action, a reality that Kumar's arrest makes starkly clear.

What Happens Next

Strategic Material Security Concerns
›Tungsten oxide valued at nearly $3 million.
›Used in armor-piercing rounds, lasers, and ceramics.
›Theft raises questions about supply chain security.
›Federal focus on critical material supply chains increasing.

Kumar faces theft charges in Pennsylvania. His immigration case will proceed separately through federal channels. The broader political fallout is likely to intensify as the Trump administration uses cases like this to build its case against California's immigration policies ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

Mitsubishi Materials has not publicly commented on the recovery of the stolen tungsten oxide shipment.
